2-5.title: Mixing Magic!
2-5.description: Let's be scientists! We can mix things together and see what happens!

en.title: Mixing Magic!
en.welcome: Put on your lab coat! Snap! Put on your goggles! Click! Today we are Chemists. We mix things!
en.mainContent:
**Everything is made of tiny bits:** Look at your hand. Look at the table. They are made of tiny, tiny blocks called **Atoms**. Too small to see!

**Mixing:** What happens when we mix things?
*   **Mix Red and Blue paint:** You get PURPLE! Magic!
*   **Mix Flour and Water:** You get sticky dough! Yuck!
*   **Mix Baking Soda and Vinegar:** FIZZ! BUBBLE! POP! It makes a volcano!

**Solids, Liquids, Gas:**
*   **Solid:** Hard like a rock.
*   **Liquid:** Wet like water.
*   **Gas:** Invisible like air. (Blow on your hand. Feel the wind? That's gas!).

**Hot and Cold:**
*   When water gets **Cold**, it turns to Ice (Solid). Brrr!
*   When water gets **Hot**, it turns to Steam (Gas). Whoosh!

**Kitchen Chemistry:** Cooking is chemistry! When you bake a cake, the gooey batter turns into a fluffy cake. The oven changes it!
keyPoints: Everything is made of tiny atoms
Mixing things can make new things (Red + Blue = Purple)
Baking Soda + Vinegar = Bubbles (Reaction)
Solids, Liquids, and Gases are different forms
Cooking is chemistry (Heat changes food)
interactionPrompts: Pretend to stir a big pot. Mix, mix, mix!
Make a fizzing sound! Pshhhhh!
Is ice a Solid or a Liquid?
en.wisdomMoment: The world is full of surprises. If you look closely, everything is magic.
en.cta: Ask a grown-up to help you mix Baking Soda and Vinegar. Watch the bubbles!
en.summary: You learned about Atoms, Mixing, Bubbles, Solids/Liquids/Gas, and Kitchen Chemistry!

6-12.title: Chemistry: The Lego Blocks of the Universe
6-12.description: Atoms, Elements, and the Periodic Table

en.title: Chemistry: The Lego Blocks of the Universe
en.welcome: Imagine if you had a Lego set that could build ANYTHING. A tree, a dog, a star, a computer. The universe is that Lego set. The blocks are called **Atoms**.
en.mainContent:
**Atoms:** The smallest unit of matter. 
*   **Protons (+):** In the center (Nucleus). Heavy.
*   **Neutrons (0):** In the center. Heavy.
*   **Electrons (-):** Buzzing around the outside. Tiny and fast.

**Elements:** Types of atoms. 
*   **Hydrogen (H):** 1 Proton. The lightest gas. Fuel for stars.
*   **Oxygen (O):** 8 Protons. We breathe it!
*   **Carbon (C):** 6 Protons. The basis of life (You are a carbon-based lifeform).
*   **Gold (Au):** 79 Protons. Shiny and heavy.

**The Periodic Table:** The chart of all elements. It organizes them by how many protons they have. It's like a menu of the universe.

**Molecules:** When atoms hold hands. 
*   **H2O (Water):** 2 Hydrogen + 1 Oxygen.
*   **CO2 (Carbon Dioxide):** 1 Carbon + 2 Oxygen. (What we breathe out).

**Chemical Reactions:** Breaking molecules and making new ones. 
*   *Fire:* Oxygen + Wood + Heat = Ash + Smoke + Light. 
*   *Rust:* Iron + Oxygen = Rust.

**Acids and Bases:**
*   **Acid:** Sour! (Lemon, Vinegar). Turns litmus paper Red.
*   **Base:** Bitter/Soapy! (Soap, Baking Soda). Turns litmus paper Blue.
*   **Neutral:** Water.
keyPoints: Atoms are made of Protons, Neutrons, and Electrons
Elements are different types of atoms (Hydrogen, Oxygen, Gold)
The Periodic Table lists all elements
Molecules are atoms bonded together (H2O)
Chemical Reactions change substances (Fire, Rust)
Acids are sour; Bases are soapy
interactionPrompts: If you split a water molecule (H2O), what do you get?
Why is Gold different from Carbon? (Different number of protons!)
Is a lemon an Acid or a Base?
en.wisdomMoment: You are made of atoms that were forged in stars. You are literally stardust.
en.cta: Look at the Periodic Table online. Find your age (Atomic Number). What element are you? (e.g., 8 = Oxygen).
en.summary: You've learned about Atoms, Elements, Periodic Table, Molecules, Reactions, and Acids/Bases.

13-17.title: Chemistry: Bonding and Reactions
13-17.description: Ionic vs Covalent bonds, Stoichiometry, and the energy of change

en.title: Chemistry: Bonding and Reactions
en.welcome: Chemistry is the study of change. How does a harmless metal (Sodium) and a poisonous gas (Chlorine) combine to make something delicious (Table Salt)? It's all about the bonds.
en.mainContent:
**The Octet Rule:** Atoms want to be happy. 'Happy' means having 8 electrons in their outer shell. They will steal or share electrons to get there.

**Types of Bonds:**
*   **Ionic Bonding (The Thief):** One atom steals an electron. Now one is (+) and one is (-). Opposites attract! They stick together like magnets. (NaCl - Salt).
*   **Covalent Bonding (The Sharer):** Atoms share electrons. They hold hands. (H2O - Water). Stronger bond.
*   **Metallic Bonding:** A sea of electrons flowing around metal atoms. This is why metals conduct electricity.

**Chemical Equations:** $2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$. 
*   **Reactants:** What you start with (Left side).
*   **Products:** What you end with (Right side).
*   **Conservation of Mass:** You can't lose atoms. If you start with 4 Hydrogens, you must end with 4 Hydrogens. Balancing equations is the math of chemistry.

**Energy in Reactions:**
*   **Exothermic:** Releases heat (Fire, Explosion). Feels hot.
*   **Endothermic:** Absorbs heat (Ice pack). Feels cold.

**Catalysts:** A helper that speeds up a reaction but doesn't get used up. (Enzymes in your spit are catalysts that break down food).

**The Mole:** A chemist's dozen. It's a huge number ($6.022 \times 10^{23}$). It helps us count atoms by weighing them.
keyPoints: Atoms bond to get a full outer shell (Octet Rule)
Ionic Bonds transfer electrons; Covalent Bonds share them
Chemical Equations must be balanced (Conservation of Mass)
Exothermic releases heat; Endothermic absorbs heat
Catalysts speed up reactions
The Mole is a unit for counting atoms
interactionPrompts: Why does salt dissolve in water? (Ionic bonds break easily in water)
Is a burning candle Exothermic or Endothermic?
Balance this: $H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow \_HCl$ (Answer: 2)
en.wisdomMoment: Change requires energy. Sometimes you have to break bonds to form new, better ones. This is true in chemistry and in life.
en.cta: Mix yeast and hydrogen peroxide (Elephant Toothpaste experiment - look it up first!). Watch the catalyst work.
en.summary: You've explored Ionic/Covalent Bonds, Equations, Exothermic/Endothermic, Catalysts, and The Mole.

18-35.title: Organic Chemistry: The Molecules of Life
18-35.description: Carbon, polymers, and the chemistry of your own body

en.title: Organic Chemistry: The Molecules of Life
en.welcome: Organic Chemistry is the study of Carbon. Why Carbon? Because it's the 'Duck Tape' of the periodic table. It can stick to almost anything, creating the complex chains necessary for life.
en.mainContent:
**Carbon's Superpower:** Carbon has 4 bonding sites. It can form rings, chains, and sheets. This versatility allows for DNA, proteins, and plastics.

**The 4 Macromolecules of Life:**
1.  **Carbohydrates (Sugars):** Energy! Glucose is fuel. Starch is stored fuel.
2.  **Lipids (Fats):** Storage and Structure. Cell membranes are made of fat. Fat stores energy for the long term.
3.  **Proteins:** The Machines. Muscles, enzymes, antibodies. Made of Amino Acids folded into complex shapes. Shape determines function.
4.  **Nucleic Acids (DNA/RNA):** Information. The code for building proteins.

**Polymers:** Plastics are long chains of carbon (Polymers). 
*   *Natural:* Rubber, Silk, Wool.
*   *Synthetic:* Nylon, Polyester, PVC.
We live in the Age of Plastics, for better or worse.

**Pharmacology:** Drugs are molecules designed to fit into specific receptors in your body (like a key in a lock). 
*   *Aspirin:* Blocks the enzyme that causes pain signals.
*   *Caffeine:* Blocks the receptor that makes you feel tired (Adenosine).

**Fermentation:** Yeast eats sugar and poops out alcohol and CO2. This gives us bread, beer, and wine. One of the oldest chemical technologies.
keyPoints: Organic Chemistry focuses on Carbon compounds
4 Macromolecules: Carbs (Energy), Lipids (Fat), Proteins (Machines), Nucleic Acids (Info)
Polymers are long chains (Plastics)
Drugs work by interacting with body receptors (Lock and Key)
Fermentation is a biological chemical reaction
interactionPrompts: Why is Carbon better for life than Silicon?
How does caffeine keep you awake?
Why are plastics so hard to break down? (Strong carbon bonds!)
en.wisdomMoment: We are chemical machines, but we are more than the sum of our parts. The magic is in the complexity, the emergence of consciousness from carbon.
en.core_metaphor: Carbon is the skeleton of life
en.cta: Look at the ingredients label of a snack. Find the Carbs, Fats, and Proteins. That's Organic Chemistry.
en.summary: You've explored Carbon, Macromolecules (Carbs/Lipids/Proteins/DNA), Polymers, Pharmacology, and Fermentation.

36-60.title: Alchemy to Chemistry: The Quest for Gold
36-60.description: The history of chemistry, from the Philosopher's Stone to the Periodic Table

en.title: Alchemy to Chemistry: The Quest for Gold
en.welcome: Before there was Chemistry, there was Alchemy. Wizards trying to turn lead into gold and find the Elixir of Life. They failed at magic, but they invented science.
en.mainContent:
**The Alchemists:** They believed matter was composed of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water. They sought the 'Philosopher's Stone' to purify matter. 
*   *Legacy:* They invented distillation, crystallization, and lab equipment (beakers, flasks). They discovered elements like Phosphorus and Mercury.

**The Skeptical Chymist (Robert Boyle):** In 1661, Boyle argued that matter is made of particles, not elements. He separated magic from measurement. Chemistry was born.

**Lavoisier and Oxygen:** Antoine Lavoisier discovered that fire isn't an element; it's a reaction with Oxygen. He proved the Conservation of Mass. (He was later beheaded in the French Revolution, a tragic loss for science).

**Mendeleev's Dream:** Dmitri Mendeleev wrote the known elements on cards. He arranged them by weight and properties. He saw a pattern. He left GAPS for undiscovered elements, predicting their properties perfectly. The Periodic Table is a map of the universe.

**Marie Curie:** The only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry). She discovered Polonium and Radium (Radioactivity). She died for her science (radiation poisoning).

**The Haber Process:** Fritz Haber figured out how to pull Nitrogen from the air to make fertilizer. This invention feeds half the world's population today. (He also invented chemical weapons. Science is a double-edged sword).
keyPoints: Alchemy was the mystical ancestor of Chemistry
Lavoisier discovered Oxygen and Conservation of Mass
Mendeleev created the Periodic Table and predicted new elements
Marie Curie pioneered Radioactivity
The Haber Process (Fertilizer) changed the world population
interactionPrompts: Why do you think Alchemists were so obsessed with Gold?
If you could discover a new element, what would you name it?
Is Fritz Haber a hero (fertilizer) or a villain (chemical weapons)?
en.wisdomMoment: Nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed. (Lavoisier). This is true for atoms, and perhaps for souls.
en.core_metaphor: Chemistry is the child of Alchemy
en.cta: Look up the symbol for 'Lead' (Pb) and 'Gold' (Au). They are close on the table! The Alchemists weren't totally crazy.
en.summary: You've explored Alchemy, Boyle, Lavoisier, Mendeleev, Curie, and the Haber Process.

61-102.title: The Chemistry of Cooking: Molecular Gastronomy
61-102.description: Understanding the reactions that make food delicious

en.title: The Chemistry of Cooking: Molecular Gastronomy
en.welcome: The kitchen is the most common laboratory. Every time you cook, you are performing chemical reactions. Let's understand the science of flavor.
en.mainContent:
**The Maillard Reaction:** The most important reaction in cooking. When amino acids (protein) and sugars react under heat (300°F+), they turn brown and create complex flavors. 
*   *Examples:* Seared steak, toasted bread, roasted coffee, chocolate. Without Maillard, food is bland.

**Caramelization:** The oxidation of sugar. When sugar gets hot, it breaks down into hundreds of new compounds (nutty, buttery, bitter). 
*   *Examples:* Caramel sauce, onions, crème brûlée.

**Emulsions:** Mixing oil and water (which hate each other). You need an emulsifier (like egg yolk or mustard) to bond them. 
*   *Examples:* Mayonnaise, Vinaigrette, Hollandaise.

**Leavening:** Making dough rise. 
*   *Biological:* Yeast eats sugar, burps CO2 bubbles (Bread).
*   *Chemical:* Baking Soda + Acid = CO2 bubbles (Cake/Pancakes).
*   *Mechanical:* Whipping air into egg whites (Soufflé).

**Denaturation:** Changing the shape of proteins. 
*   *Heat:* Cooking an egg (clear becomes white).
*   *Acid:* Ceviche (lime juice 'cooks' the fish).

**Taste vs. Flavor:** 
*   *Taste:* Tongue (Sweet, Sour, Salty, Bitter, Umami).
*   *Flavor:* Tongue + Nose (Aroma). 80% of flavor is smell. Hold your nose and eat a strawberry; it tastes like sugar, not strawberry.
keyPoints: Maillard Reaction creates browning and flavor (Steak/Toast)
Caramelization is the browning of sugar
Emulsions mix oil and water (Mayo)
Leavening creates bubbles to make food fluffy
Denaturation changes protein texture (Cooking eggs)
Flavor is mostly smell
interactionPrompts: Why does boiled meat taste different than roasted meat? (No Maillard reaction in water!)
What happens if you forget the baking powder in a cake?
Try eating something while holding your nose. What happens?
en.wisdomMoment: Cooking is an act of love made visible. It is chemistry for the soul. Feed people well.
en.cta: Toast a piece of bread. Watch it turn brown. Smell the change. That is the Maillard Reaction in action.
en.summary: You've explored Maillard Reaction, Caramelization, Emulsions, Leavening, Denaturation, and Taste vs. Flavor.
